purpose: This tool lets you move, stretch and flip a graph by changing numbers in a formula. By tracking one point you see exactly what each number does, so you can read a transformation straight from its formula.

stops.title: Two graphs, one point
stops.text: The grey curve is the base function f. The blue curve is the transformed g. The ringed point P sits on f. Its red twin P' shows where P lands on g. Drag P along the grey curve.
stops.try: Drag P to the left and right. Notice how P' follows.

stops.title: Base function
stops.text: Pick which simple graph you start with: absolute value, square, cube, square root or sine. All four sliders below then change that graph.
stops.try: Choose sin x, then change b.

stops.title: h: shift right
stops.text: A number inside the brackets with x. Positive h moves the whole graph right. This feels backwards, since the formula says x minus h. Compare P and P' to see it.
stops.try: Slide h to 2 and see which way P' moves.

stops.title: k: shift up
stops.text: A number added outside. Every point moves up by k, and down if k is negative. This one is not backwards.
stops.try: Set k to 1 and read P' against P.

stops.title: a: stretch and flip
stops.text: Multiplies every height. Bigger than 1 makes it taller, between 0 and 1 squashes it, and negative flips it upside down across the x-axis.

stops.title: b: squeeze and flip
stops.text: Multiplies x inside the brackets. Bigger than 1 squeezes the graph sideways, and negative flips it left to right. It is the opposite of a, since it divides the x-distances.
stops.try: Slide b to 2 and watch P' move toward the y-axis.

stops.title: Reset
stops.text: Puts a, b, h and k back to the plain base graph, so the blue curve lies on the grey one. Your chosen base function stays.

stops.title: What Next does
stops.text: Step 1 shows both graphs equal. Step 2 sets h and k. Step 3 adds a. Step 4 switches to sine with b. Each is a setting you can change.

teacher: Ask students to predict where P' lands before changing a slider, then check. Good question: why does a plus inside the brackets move the graph left? Common misconception: thinking h and b act like k and a, when they act on x and work backwards.
